title: Act II, Scene IV

teacherSummary.text: Ross and an Old Man describe unnatural events: darkness by day, a falcon killed by a 'mousing owl', and Duncan's horses breaking loose and eating each other. Macduff reports that the princes are suspected of bribing the grooms, that Macbeth has been named king and has gone to Scone to be invested, and that Duncan's body has been carried to Colmekill. Macduff will not go to Scone but home to Fife.

context.history: The idea of a 'great chain of being' held that a king's murder disordered nature; Holinshed's chronicle supplied the omens of the horses and the darkness.

significance: The omens turn the murder into a cosmic crime. Macduff's quiet refusal to attend the coronation is the first sign of resistance.
discussionQuestions: Do you think the natural world reflects human events? Why do stories so often say it does?
Where does imagery appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with fate and free will?

satQuestions.passage:
Threescore and ten I can remember well:
Within the volume of which time I have seen
Hours dreadful and things strange; but this sore night
Hath trifled former knowings.
Ah, good father,
Thou seest, the heavens, as troubled with man’s act,
Threaten his bloody stage: by the clock, ’tis day,
And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp:
Is’t night’s predominance, or the day’s shame,
That darkness does the face of earth entomb,
When living light should kiss it?
’Tis unnatural,
Even like the deed that’s done. On Tuesday last,
A falcon, towering in her pride of place,
Was by a mousing owl hawk’d at and kill’d.
And Duncan’s horses—a thing most strange and certain—
Beauteous and swift, the minions of their race,
Turn’d wild in nature, broke their stalls, flung out,
Contending ’gainst obedience, as they would make
War with mankind.
’Tis said they eat each other.
They did so, to the amazement of mine eyes
That look’d upon’t. Here comes the good Macduff.

claimEvidenceReasoning.evidence: by the clock, ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp
claimEvidenceReasoning.reasoning: Ross sees that "dark night strangles the travelling lamp" by day, and a falcon is killed by "a mousing owl," a lower creature overthrowing a higher, just as Macbeth killed his king.

weDoAnswers: The falcon is the king, the owl Macbeth. It shows the belief in a divine order (the "great chain of being").
analysis.weDoWords: “Falcon”, “towering” and “mousing owl” stand out. A small owl that hunts mice kills a high-flying falcon, an unnatural reversal that pictures a lesser man killing a king.
analysis.weDoQ2: The Old Man reports an omen in nature, so the line suggests that the murder has upset the whole order of the world, not only one family.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “by the clock, ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp” slowly and put it in my own words: Ross says that by the clock it is day, yet dark night strangles the sun. Next, craft. I notice the violent verb "strangles," applied to night killing daylight. The strongest word is “strangles”: it makes the darkness a murderer, echoing Duncan's death. Then, effect. What does Ross notice about the unnatural darkness? My answer: Ross notices that the unnatural darkness covers the day after the king's murder; nature itself seems disordered, which shows that the crime has upset the whole order of the world.
